Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We report observations of the dust cloud L1204 with the Onsala 25-m telescope in the 6 cm (1$_{11}-1_{10}$) transition of \htco. The observed region includes the   S140 H${\alpha}$ arc. This spectral line is seen here in absorption against the cosmic microwave background, indicating the presence of widespread warm molecular gas at intermediate densities. Overall, the distributions of H$_2$CO and CO (taken from the literature) are fairly similar, though significant differences exist at small scales. Most notably, while the CO peak is nearly coincident with the S140 H${\alpha}$ arc, the maximum H$_2$CO absorption is clearly separated from it by a full 10$'$ beam ($\sim$ 3 pc). We argue that these differences result from differing abundances and excitation requirements. The CO(1-0) line is more optically thick and more biased towards warm gas than the H$_2$CO 6 cm line. On the other hand, formaldehyde is more easily photodissociated and is, therefore, a poorer tracer of the molecular gas located immediately behind Photon Dominated Regions.

outputs.L1: We present observations of the L1204 dust cloud obtained with the Onsala 25-m telescope in the 6 cm (1$_{11}$–1$_{10}$) transition of \htco. The observed region encompasses the S140 H${\alpha}$ arc. The spectral line appears in absorption against the cosmic microwave background, indicating the presence of widespread, warm molecular gas at intermediate densities. Overall, the distributions of H$_2$CO and CO—the latter taken from the literature—are broadly similar, although significant differences emerge on small scales. Most notably, whereas the CO peak is nearly coincident with the S140 H${\alpha}$ arc, the maximum H$_2$CO absorption is clearly offset from it by one full 10$'$ beam ($\sim$3 pc). We argue that these differences arise from variations in abundance and excitation requirements. The CO(1–0) line is more optically thick and more strongly biased toward warm gas than the H$_2$CO 6 cm line. Conversely, formaldehyde is more readily photodissociated and is therefore a poorer tracer of molecular gas located immediately behind Photon Dominated Regions.
outputs.L2: Using the Onsala 25-m telescope, we mapped the L1204 dust cloud in the 6 cm \(1_{11}-1_{10}\) transition of \(\mathrm{H_2CO}\), covering an area that contains the S140 H\(\alpha\) arc. The line appears in absorption against the cosmic microwave background, revealing extended warm molecular material with intermediate gas densities. On large scales, the H\(_2\)CO distribution broadly resembles published CO maps, but the two tracers differ substantially on smaller scales. In particular, the CO maximum lies close to the S140 H\(\alpha\) arc, whereas the strongest H\(_2\)CO absorption is displaced from the arc by an entire \(10'\) beam, corresponding to approximately 3 pc. We attribute these contrasts to differences in molecular abundance and excitation conditions. Compared with the 6 cm H\(_2\)CO transition, CO(1–0) has a higher optical depth and preferentially traces warmer gas. Formaldehyde, however, is more susceptible to photodissociation, making it less effective for tracing molecular material directly behind photon-dominated regions.
outputs.L3:
The L1204 dust cloud was observed with the Onsala 25-m telescope using the 6 cm transition of formaldehyde (H₂CO). The observations covered the region surrounding the S140 Hα arc. The H₂CO line was detected in absorption against the cosmic microwave background, indicating that warm molecular gas at intermediate densities is widespread throughout the cloud.

On large scales, the spatial distributions of H₂CO and carbon monoxide (CO) are broadly similar. However, significant differences emerge at smaller spatial scales. In particular, the strongest H₂CO absorption is offset from the CO emission peak near the S140 Hα arc by approximately 10 arcminutes, corresponding to a projected distance of about 3 pc.

These differences can be attributed to a combination of molecular abundance and excitation effects. The CO(1–0) transition is more optically thick and therefore tends to emphasize warmer gas. By contrast, H₂CO is more readily photodissociated by ultraviolet radiation, making it a poor tracer of molecular material located directly behind photon-dominated regions. Consequently, although both molecules trace the general structure of L1204, their detailed distributions reflect different physical and chemical conditions within the cloud.
outputs.L4:
The L1204 dark cloud was observed with the Onsala 25-m radio telescope in the 6 cm absorption line of formaldehyde (H₂CO). The mapped region included the prominent Hα emission arc associated with S140, where ultraviolet radiation from nearby massive stars illuminates and interacts with the molecular cloud. The H₂CO measurements were compared with previously published CO observations to examine how well the two molecules trace the distribution and physical conditions of the molecular gas.

On large scales, the H₂CO absorption generally follows the CO emission, confirming that formaldehyde traces much of the same cloud material. However, the strongest H₂CO absorption is displaced from the CO maximum and the S140 ionization front by roughly 3 pc. In particular, H₂CO does not trace the gas immediately behind the photon-dominated region as effectively as CO.

This difference is likely caused by a combination of radiative-transfer and chemical effects. Variations in optical depth and excitation can alter the apparent strengths of the H₂CO and CO lines, while ultraviolet radiation near the cloud surface can photodissociate formaldehyde or otherwise reduce its abundance. Consequently, although 6 cm H₂CO absorption is useful for mapping colder and more shielded molecular material, it appears to be a less reliable tracer than CO of gas located directly behind strongly irradiated photon-dominated regions.

The area combines natural beauty with a rich maritime history, making it attractive to residents and visitors alike. counterfactuals.output: We present Onsala 25-m observations of the L1204 molecular cloud in the 4.83-GHz \(1_{10}-1_{11}\) transition of formaldehyde. H\(_2\)CO is detected in absorption over the principal cloud complex, with the strongest features associated with the dense material near S140. Comparison with published CO maps shows that the formaldehyde distribution follows the main CO velocity components and large-scale cloud morphology, but is more concentrated toward regions of high molecular column density. The results indicate that 6-cm H\(_2\)CO absorption is an effective tracer of the denser, colder structure within L1204.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the key results of a study mapping H₂CO absorption toward the S140 Hα arc, including the physical interpretation of its offset from the CO peak.
counterfactuals.output:
- Mapping of the 6-cm \(1_{10}-1_{11}\) H\(_2\)CO line detected widespread, anomalous absorption across the molecular cloud adjoining the S140 H\(\alpha\) bright rim. Its velocity and line-width structure agreed with the associated CO cloud, confirming that the absorption arises in the same foreground molecular material rather than in unrelated gas.

- The H\(_2\)CO absorption was concentrated in a ridge near the ionization/photodissociation front, but its strongest absorption did not coincide with the maximum CO integrated intensity; it was displaced toward the H\(\alpha\) arc.

- The offset was interpreted primarily as an excitation and cloud-structure effect, not as evidence that H\(_2\)CO and CO belong to different clouds. The 6-cm transition is strongest in absorption in moderately dense, subthermally excited gas. Deeper toward the CO peak, where column density and density are higher, collisions drive the H\(_2\)CO excitation temperature upward and reduce the line contrast. Compression and UV processing at the illuminated cloud surface may also enhance the H\(_2\)CO-rich layer. Thus the absorption peak traces the cooler, moderately dense interface/foreground envelope, whereas the CO peak more nearly marks the largest total molecular column.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft an abstract explaining why 6 cm H₂CO and CO(1–0) trace different structures in the L1204 molecular cloud, with attention to optical depth, excitation, and photodissociation.
counterfactuals.output: **Abstract—**We examine the contrasting structures traced by the 6 cm \(1_{11}\!-\!1_{10}\) K-doublet transition of formaldehyde (H\(_2\)CO) and the \(J=1\!-\!0\) line of CO in the L1204 molecular cloud. The morphological differences do not necessarily imply distinct gas components, but arise from the lines’ different radiative-transfer and chemical sensitivities. CO(1–0) is readily excited in widespread, relatively low-density molecular gas and is generally optically thick, so its brightness primarily reflects excitation temperature and beam filling factor rather than total column density; foreground material can also produce self-absorption. In contrast, the 6 cm H\(_2\)CO line is commonly collisionally anti-inverted and observed in absorption against the cosmic microwave background or local radio continuum. Its visibility therefore depends strongly on density, H\(_2\)CO column per unit velocity, line-of-sight continuum, and the excitation temperature relative to the background. It preferentially emphasizes moderately dense, shielded structures while remaining weak or absent where excitation approaches the background temperature. Chemistry further separates the tracers: CO self-shields effectively and can remain abundant through much of a cloud envelope, whereas H\(_2\)CO is more readily photodissociated in far-ultraviolet-illuminated gas and is concentrated in regions with sufficient dust shielding or active grain-surface chemistry. Thus, CO(1–0) maps the warm, optically thick molecular envelope and cloud surfaces, while 6 cm H\(_2\)CO absorption highlights selected shielded density enhancements and foreground layers. The observed discrepancies in L1204 are therefore a combined consequence of optical-depth saturation, non-LTE excitation, background-continuum geometry, and differential photochemistry.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.output:
Using the Onsala 25-m telescope, observers mapped the 4.83-GHz \(1_{10}-1_{11}\) transition of formaldehyde toward the dark cloud L1204, which contains the bright-rimmed region S140. The line appeared in absorption—largely against the diffuse radio background/CMB—and followed the molecular-cloud velocity rather than the optically bright rim.

The deepest H\(_2\)CO absorption was not located at the S140 Hα arc, the ionization and photon-dominated-region boundary. Instead, it lay about **3 pc in projected distance farther into L1204**. Thus the formaldehyde maximum marks cool, shielded molecular material well behind the illuminated surface, rather than the thin interface itself.

This offset is important when interpreting formaldehyde maps of bright-rimmed clouds: centimeter-wave H\(_2\)CO absorption can probe substantial columns of dense molecular gas behind a PDR, even where optical tracers reveal only the front surface. Consequently, an H\(_2\)CO absorption peak should not automatically be identified with the PDR or ionization front; it may trace the cloud’s deeper, colder interior.
